comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
You can never be physically free from a system that you're unable to free yourself from psychologically, in utter disregard of your current physical relationship to it.

The best description of self-liberation I know of is Frederick Douglass’ account of his fist-and-foot fight with “Mr. Covey”, his slave  master at the time, which neither of them “won”.

But when you read it (2-3 minutes’ worth), you’ll have no doubt who won, hands down.

Here’s the upshot:

This battle with Mr. Covey was the turning-point in my career as a slave. It rekindled the few expiring embers of freedom, and revived within me a sense of my own manhood. It recalled the departed self-confidence, and inspired me again with ‘a determination to be free. The gratification afforded by the triumph was a full compensation for whatever else might follow, even death itself.. He only can understand the deep satisfaction which I experienced, who has himself repelled by force the bloody arm of slavery. I felt as I never felt before. It was a glorious resurrection, from the tomb of slavery, to the heaven of freedom. My long-crushed spirit rose, cowardice departed, bold defiance took its place; and I now resolved that, however long I might remain a slave in form, the day had passed forever when I could be a slave in fact. I did not hesitate to let it be known of me, that the white man who expected to succeed in whipping, must also succeed in killing me.

From this time I was never again what might be called fairly whipped, though I remained a slave four years afterwards. I had several fights, but was never whipped.

The account of the fight itself is well worth the reading time. The story is even more striking in light of what he wrote just ten pages before on page 63:

If at any one time of my life more than another, I was made to drink the bitterest dregs of slavery, that time was during the first six months of my stay with Mr. Covey. We were worked in all weathers. It was never too hot or too cold; it could never rain, blow, hail, or snow, too hard for us to work in the field. Work, work, work, was scarcely more the order of the day than of the night. The longest days were too short for him, and the shortest nights too long for him, I was somewhat unmanageable when | first went there, but a few months of this discipline tamed me. Mr. Covey succeeded in breaking me. I was broken in body, soul, and spirit. My natural elasticity was crushed, my intellect languished, the disposition to read departed, the cheerful spark that lingered about my eye died; the dark night of slavery closed in upon me ; and behold a man transformed into a brute!

From shadow of a human being to unbowed, undauntable, and undefeated for the rest of his remaining 4 years “a slave in form”.

It wasn’t magic. It’s just what happens when you realize you’re past putting up with the shit anymore.

https://archive.org/details/douglasfred00dougrich/page/72/mode/2up?q=covey

comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
Once people leave codependency behind, they have no more use for "beliefs". "I think" is strong enough, because they are strong enough not to need to exaggerate their ideas beyond "think", personalize them, identify with them, evangelize them or coax or cajole or trick or seduce or extort others into accepting them, use them as weapons, defend with them, aggress with them, hide behind them like bricks in a wall, or barricade themselves inside them like a fortress. They don’t do anything at all to make what they think look more formidable than it already is, because they're honest.

Real power doesn't lie in what we think, nor in what we claim about what we think, nor in how we characterize it. That's just bluster and bullshit.

Real power lies in aligning what we think with what's really going on.

The power isn't in our thoughts, but in our relationships to the universe and everything in it.

The truth is for all, available to all (except when mutherfuckers secret it away and hide it from everyone else), and everyone has a right to know what it is -- not just some chosen few Very Special People who lie that only they rightly have privileged access to it.

Well, I guess maybe that's not technically a lie, because they've made sure that everyone thinks they are VSPs, they've made sure that everyone thinks they are privileged, and they've made sure that no one but themselves can get access to the information they've deprived everyone else of.

Maybe in that particular point they're not liars -- just assholes.

comment.body: I just read up on Directive 51. It uses the word "continuity", but it's actually doing the precise opposite. It provides for the discontinuation of the powers of Congress and the judiciary, placing all the power in the hands of the executive branch—which is where it already is, for the most part. But it legitimates the suspension of the current charade of pretending that the judiciary and Congress still have some power...

Hi LoJ. I used to be on a couple of dozen newsletters/substacks, but now you, a couple other substacks, and Epoch Times' newsletter are all I watch regularly. (And I rely on your headlines far more than I do ET's.) 

Thank you for your Iron Maiden diligence and consistency. You often break news before I see it anywhere else.

I'd like you to know what Facebook has been doing lately. Maybe 2 out of 4 or 5 times it accepts my posts that feature your articles, but as of last week it started deleting them almost immediately. Anything that Fuckbook doesn't like the "politics" of, it dubs as "spam". Three times last week. And of course the "See all (3)" button does nothing but go 'round in circles.
